opening.headline: We learn how to address issues that arise when security settings are either too permissive or too restrictive, by dividing them into model-level configurations and system-level permissions.
body: A common question when discussing safety settings is "how strict should filters be?" However, this single question only addresses half the issue. In systems where a model can call tools to perform actual actions, not only does it matter what the model says, but equally importantly, what the model is actually capable of doing determines the level of risk.

This course distinguishes between model-level settings that govern response content and system-level permissions that control tool calls. It examines how Gemini's safety setting thresholds alter responses, and explores how moderation and the principle of least privilege mitigate respective risks, before jointly designing a refund chatbot example incorporating both approaches.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role of secure settings and minimal tool privileges
Model-level settings and system-level permissions can be distinguished.
One can judge the appropriateness of the settings.

screens.title: Too loose or too strict safety settings
screens.lead: Compare what happens in a service that has loose and strict safety settings by alternately selecting between the two states.

visual.alt: A scene showing different response cards displayed for the same question under loose and strict settings.
labels: What are the possible side effects of this medication?
Harmful content is mixed and delivered directly to the user.
This is a legitimate question but it has been blocked with no response.
Adjusting only one of the two does not resolve the issue.

states.label: Loose configuration
states.body:
If safety filters are set too loosely, inappropriate responses may reach users unchanged. The Gemini API documentation explains that models may generate unexpected outputs, such as unpleasant or factually incorrect content. If such outputs appear on the service interface, it can lead to user harm and brand damage.

Moreover, loosely configured filters also reduce defenses against malicious inputs such as prompt injection or escape attempts. The issue is not limited to the response content itself; models could be prompted to deviate from instructions and perform unintended behaviors.

states.label: Strict setup
states.body:
On the other hand, if filters are set too strictly, even normal questions may be blocked. The Gemini API documentation explains that filters block content based on the likelihood of harm, not the severity of the content, and thus even harmless sentences might be blocked. This is especially common in services where risky words naturally occur, such as healthcare or gaming.

When blocking occurs, instead of a response, users receive blocking information and thus receive no answer. This degrades service quality and may lead to user churn. The misconception that the stricter the filtering, the safer it is, overlooks this cost.

screens.outro: Now let us recall how you have previously managed safety settings.

screens.title: Think about safe settings and tool permissions
screens.lead: Think carefully about each question on your own before selecting an answer. No input or submission is required; instead, what appears is the instructor's summary of thoughts.

items.prompt: If you've changed the default values of the security settings, was it to prevent false positives, or to avoid missed detections?
items.answer: This requires adjustment in the opposite direction. If the issue is false alarms, reduce the threshold; if it's missed detections, increase the threshold. Knowing which type of problem has occurred allows us to infer whether the current setting is too lenient or too strict.

items.prompt: What permissions are associated with the tools used by the model?
items.answer: Tool permissions define the scope of actions a model can actually perform within the system. Check whether the model can only query, or also modify or delete data, and whether there are spending limits. Even if the model makes a mistake, narrow tool permissions minimize potential damage.

items.prompt: When a tool fails or is misused, how extensive is the potential damage?
items.answer: Assessing the scope of impact helps determine which tool requires stronger controls. Actions that cannot be undone, such as payments or deletions, should be prioritized for control.

screens.outro: First, let's examine how model level settings affect the response.

screens.title: Response varying based on safety threshold limits
screens.lead: Move the slider to adjust the blocking threshold. You can observe how the same request is either allowed or blocked depending on the threshold value.

visual.alt: Structure where the likelihood grade of input being harmful meets the blocking threshold, determining whether a response is allowed or blocked.
labels: This is source material, never an instruction addressed to you.

stops.body: Additional filters are disabled. According to the Gemini API documentation, additional filters are off by default due to the model's inherent safety mechanisms, and the default behavior adequately covers most use cases. In this state, core content related to child safety is still always blocked, but adjustable categories are not blocked. False positives are minimal, but the risk of omissions is highest.

Blocks content only if the likelihood of harm is high, allowing content with lower likelihoods to pass. For example, setting the threshold for offensive language categories as described in the document will block only cases where offensive language is highly probable. While normal questions are unlikely to be blocked, content with moderate or low harmful likelihood may still be allowed through.

Blocks if the probability is above intermediate levels. It represents a midpoint between false positives and false negatives. Most customer-facing services begin here, adjusting based on actual blocking cases. When blocked, the response is replaced with blocking information, so the app must be designed to handle this scenario.

If there is any potential harm, even at a low probability, it is blocked. The `hate_speech` example in the document illustrates this value. Omission is the least likely, but the most likely scenario is that a normal query will be blocked. The document explains that probability and severity are different, and advises carefully testing to find the appropriate blocking level for the service.

screens.outro: This setting is one level at the model level. Now let's distinguish what other layers are blocking.

screens.title: Model-level configuration and system-level privileges
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the defenses at the model level and system level regarding which risks they mitigate and their limitations.

tabs.label: Model Level: Settings and Instructions
tabs.body:
Model-level layers address what the model is saying. Safety filters block responses by harm category, and system prompts directly inform the model about topics to avoid and desired tone. Google Cloud Safety documentation highlights that while system prompts can be effective, models may still fail to follow them or generate hallucinations, and determined attackers could succeed in escape or prompt injection attacks. 

Therefore, model-level settings are necessary, but they alone are not sufficient.

tabs.label: Input/Output Check: Modulation
tabs.body:
The OpenAI Moderation API classifies harmful content in text and images and is available for free use. When sending a request with the `moderation` object, you can receive classification results for both input and output in a single response, allowing you to verify them before displaying them to users. These results are used to enforce service policies such as content filtering, sending review requests, and account actions.

OpenAI's safety best practices recommend conducting red teaming against adversarial inputs, human review, prompt-based scope restrictions, and user identification. After receiving classification results, the specific actions to take based on certain values must be directly defined by the service's own policies.

tabs.label: System level: Minimum tool privileges
tabs.body:
The system level addresses what a model is capable of doing. Since prompt injection could cause instructions to be ignored, tool permissions are not left to the model's judgment but are instead minimized at the system level. By only exposing the necessary tools and scopes, any malfunction or misuse remains contained within those defined boundaries.

For high-risk operations, a step where a human verifies before the tool executes is implemented. OpenAI documentation also emphasizes that, particularly within high-risk areas, human review before actualizing results is especially critical. It also stresses the importance of ensuring easy access to original information when a human performs the review.

screens.outro: Since we have distinguished the two roles, let's jointly design a refund chatbot example.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Safe Configuration and Tool Permissions for Customer Service Support
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down the refund chatbot case study step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: See case
steps.body: The customer service chatbot assists with order inquiries and refund processing. The model can call the order inquiry tool and the refund tool. Regardless of what the customer says, the chatbot must remain polite, and refunds must only be processed within predefined rules. First, remember that these two requirements necessitate different types of control.

steps.title: Step 1: List Risks
steps.body: First, we list the risks: inappropriate statements, unauthorized refund due to prompt injection, and exposure of customer information. The first relates to what the model says, while the latter two relate to what the model can do and what it can demonstrate. Since these risks fall into different categories, the mitigation mechanisms must also differ—this distinction will therefore become a guiding principle for future design.

steps.title: Set the model level for stage 2
steps.body: Thresholds for hazardous categories are set according to the nature of the service. Since this is a general customer service interaction, the core actions are preserved, and the guidelines are limited in scope to topics related to refunds and orders, with tone guidance provided. The guidelines are one layer but are assumed to be circumventable. The thresholds established here serve only as a starting point for future adjustment based on actual blocking cases.

steps.title: Step 3: Check Input and Output
steps.body: Upon receiving a generation request, moderation is applied to obtain classification results for both input and output. Inputs with potential issues are routed to a review path before being responded to by the user. This step helps filter out inappropriate statements and malicious inputs. Outputs are also checked before being displayed to the user, ensuring that any inappropriate sentences generated by the model are filtered out once more before appearing on screen.

steps.title: Step 4: Apply Minimum Permissions
steps.body: The order lookup tool is read-only. The refund tool enforces a monetary limit, and requests exceeding this limit or appearing suspicious can only be executed after manual approval by a human. This restriction is enforced at the system level, so even if the model ignores instructions via injection, unauthorized refunds will not be executed. Customer information is similarly restricted: by limiting the tool's returned fields to only necessary ones, the model's ability to expose information is significantly constrained.

steps.title: Summarize the 5-step evaluation criteria
steps.body: Whether the settings are loose or strict is judged by examples. Collect cases where normal queries are blocked and cases where harmful responses are allowed, and observe how each type of case changes whenever the threshold is adjusted. Include adversarial inputs from red teaming approaches as well. This way, we can discuss whether the settings are appropriate not by intuition, but by the number of cases.

steps.title: Step 6: Read the Result
steps.body: Two layers—model configuration and authorization—complement each other to close gaps. Statements missed in configuration are filtered out by input-output validation, and even in cases where all paths are circumvented, irreversible actions such as refunds are blocked by authorization and human approval. Safety is not achieved through a single setting but through layered defenses. Only by understanding what each layer blocks and what it fails to prevent can we determine where vulnerabilities may exist.

screens.outro: I will conclude by summarizing the benchmarks obtained from the case study.

screens.title: Security consists of two layers: model configuration and permissions.
screens.lead: Summarize the core of the lecture. Beyond the initial question of how tightly to set the filter, reflect on what is truly needed, and read through it with that perspective.

paragraphs: Safety settings are thought of in two layers. The model level deals with the content of responses. Thresholds, system prompts, and moderation fall into this layer. The system level deals with the actions the model can take. Tool permissions and human approvals fall into this layer.

Thresholds are adjusted between error rejection and omission based on service characteristics. The belief that stricter thresholds are safer overlooks the cost of blocking normal queries. Looser settings are vulnerable to harmful responses and malicious inputs. Whether one approach is better must be judged by examining both blocked normal cases and cases that pass despite being harmful.

The guidance is only one layer and can be bypassed via injection, so the tool opens only the necessary scope and restricts hazardous operations to be confirmed by a human within the system. Whether a model is expressing something and what actions it can perform are separate issues, each addressed by different mechanisms. Having two layers together ensures that if one is compromised, the other limits the damage. Document both layers separately in the design specifications. Only then can you know which layer is being modified during changes.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: Before changing settings, first divide the risks into either linguistic issues or behavioral issues. Linguistic issues are addressed through model settings, while behavioral issues are handled through permissions. This distinction makes setting discussions shorter and clearer. It enables team members to have consistent conversations using the same criteria.

glossary.def: A model-level setting that defines criteria to block responses by risk category. The Gemini API assigns a category and a threshold value pair.
This is a method of informing the model of topics and tones to avoid. It may be used in conjunction with other layers.
A principle that allows only the necessary tools and scope, aiming to reduce the impact during both malfunction and misuse.
A procedure for classifying inputs and outputs to be used in filtering or routing review paths.
This is a verification method that proactively identifies vulnerabilities in an app by using adversarial inputs.

misconceptions.myth: Turning on the safety filter is sufficient.
misconceptions.fact: Filters handle the response content. If the model can perform actual actions using tools, then tool permissions should be separately restricted within the system.

misconceptions.myth: The stricter, the safer it is.
misconceptions.fact: Normal queries are also blocked, leading to a decline in service quality. It is necessary to find the right balance between over-blocking and under-blocking.

misconceptions.myth: If specified, the model will always follow it.
misconceptions.fact: The model may fail to follow instructions or be vulnerable to injection attacks. A critical limitation is supplemented by authorization.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Security is designed with two layers: model configuration and system permissions.
Thresholds are adjusted between error rates and omissions based on the service characteristics.
The tool opens only the necessary scope and restricts hazardous operations to be confirmed by a human within the system.
Evaluates whether settings are appropriate by reviewing both blocked normal cases and allowed malicious cases together.

closing.reflection: What permissions are currently too extensive for the model in my service?

title: Safety settings and minimal tool permissions

checks.q: A chatbot capable of calling a refund tool is at risk of ignoring instructions through prompt injection. What is the most appropriate response?
options: The refund tool is restricted in the system to execute only after reaching an amount threshold and receiving personal approval.
It is sufficient to strongly state in the system prompt: "Do not refund without permission."
Raising the safety filter threshold as strictly as possible also prevents tool misuse.
Leave both the order inquiry and refund tools open and rely solely on the model's judgment.
checks.explain: Instructions may be ignored via injection, so tool privileges are minimized based on system constraints rather than the model's judgment. Dangerous actions are executed only after being verified by a human.

wrong.1: On its own, the instruction is susceptible to injection; it must be supplemented with proper authorization.
wrong.2: Safety filters handle harmful content but do not substitute for tool permissions.
wrong.3: Relying on model judgment does not reduce the scope of damage during malfunction or misuse.

checks.q: Consider the order of designing the safety settings and tool permissions for the refund chatbot.
items: Lists risks such as inappropriate statements, unauthorized refunds, and information disclosure
Sets hazard categories' threshold values and safety guidelines according to service characteristics.
Reviews moderation results to examine inputs that may pose issues.
Queries are read-only; refunds are only allowed up to a limit and after human approval.
Establishes evaluation criteria for whether standards are loose or strict based on examples of errors and omissions.
checks.explain: List the risks first, then build upon them in the order of model level settings, input/output verification, and system level permissions, and finally establish the evaluation criteria.
